subject: Clarification on token accounting for long-context product lookups

Subject: Clarify per-token accounting for very long product contexts

Jordan —

Thanks again for the demo last week. One follow-up from our engineering team: we need a clear, example-driven explanation of how Redwood will bill for requests that include very long product catalogs as context. Our use case: a shopper search hits a product embedding + retrieval flow and we send the full retrieved document (often 7k–20k chars) as a single prompt. Specific questions:

- Is billing measured strictly by generated + prompt tokens, or do you apply segmentation/windowing for long context docs?
- How does rounding/minimums apply? Our contract mentions a per-call minimum unit (we thought it was 32 tokens) and then per-token billing after—examples would help.
- If we use prefix caching (same product text reused across requests), do we see credits or amortization across calls?

I've attached a few real prompt examples from our devs to illustrate the patterns. Can you provide a sample calculation (best and worst case) and indicate any knobs we can use (batching, KV reuse) to lower unit cost?

Appreciate a short write-up we can share with procurement.

Thanks,
Rajiv
Director of Engineering
LumenRetail

From: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>

Rajiv —

Thanks for the examples, that helps. Below is a concise breakdown plus two worked examples using your samples. Happy to hop on a call if you want the math walked through.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- We bill on tokenized input + output. For very long input documents we apply context segmentation for execution but billing is based on the tokenized bytes sent to the model runtime.
- Minimum quantum: tokens are billed in 64-token quanta for the current SKU on your pilot (we can confirm final contract wording). That means any partial quantum is rounded up to the next 64.
- Session amortization & KV reuse: when the same exact input prefix is cached (KV cache), we do not re-charge for cached KV tokens for subsequent streaming generation requests within the same session window; instead, we apply a per-call amortization credit. This lowers your effective per-call billed tokens when KV reuse is high.

Worked examples (using your prompt A — ~3,400 characters):
- Tokenize prompt A -> ~550 tokens (approx). Generation expected ~120 tokens. Raw sum = 670 tokens.
- Apply quantum rounding: 670/64 = 10.47 -> rounded up to 11 quanta = 11 * 64 = 704 billed tokens.
- If prompt A is identical to a cached prefix and reused in the same session: KV credit applies - we offset cached prefix tokens (example offset = 400 tokens) then bill only the delta + generation. So billed = (670 - 400) rounded to quantum -> 270 -> rounded up to 320 (5 quanta) = 320 tokens.

Edge case (very large doc split):
- If you send a 6,500-token document, we will stream the document to the model in segments for execution but tokens sent are counted in aggregate. 6,500 + generation 200 = 6,700 -> rounding to 6,752 (105 quanta). For extremely large inputs we recommend either: 1) client-side compression/truncation to only the relevant retrieved slices, or 2) use our caching/embedding flow where you store doc embeddings and only send the short retrieval summary.

Practical levers to reduce cost:
- Deduplicate/reuse identical prefixes to benefit from KV amortization.
- Batch similar requests (e.g., synchronous batched inference) so the per-request quantum rounding is amortized across more tokens.
- Use short retrieval summaries instead of pushing full product pages.

I've attached an annotated pricing table and a short example sheet that walks through these numbers for your three sample prompts. If you want, Vanessa and I can propose a one-time pilot credit to smooth the first month while you test KV reuse patterns.

This is very helpful, thank you. Two quick follow-ups after reviewing the spreadsheet:

1) Streaming case: if we open a long-lived streaming session where the client sends retrieval slices and the model emits partial answers continuously, does the 64-token quantum apply per HTTP request/chunk or to the entire streaming session? Example: we send 10 small retrieval slices (each 80–120 tokens) in separate frames within one stream and generate 50 tokens across the session. How will rounding be applied?

2) KV credit persistence: what is the TTL for a cached KV prefix to be eligible for amortization? Is it session-scoped only, or can we get multi-minute persistence across multiple user interactions (we operate chat-like sessions that last 10–15 minutes)?
